sections.title: The Sides
sections.headline: America Is Still on the Bears
sections.sub: Most-bet spreads, tickets and money
paras: Start where the crowd starts. The Bears, subject of this desk's first NFL issue, remain the most public side in football — first in tickets, second in money, at the 93-and-91-percent levels a national betting column called one of the biggest figures of the season. Behind them, the tickets and dollars tell slightly different stories. The ticket list adds the Lions laying a touchdown and the Broncos catching points on Monday night; the money list drops both and adds a road underdog — the Colts, catching three and a half in Baltimore — plus the Cowboys, whose spread money has been running north of ninety percent all week.

And then there is the number two on the money list: Pittsburgh, laying five on BetMGM's board against Atlanta. The story is not the Falcons. The story is that the public's second-biggest position of opening weekend is Aaron Rodgers, at forty-two years old, in his twenty-second season, laying points in his Pittsburgh debut. Some bets are analysis. That one is a memory.

That last one completes a remarkable picture. Jets-Titans carries the lowest total on the board — and the public is on it three different ways at once: Titans minus the points on the tickets list, Jets plus money on the dog list, and the under as the most-bet total in football. America has surrounded the worst game of the week from every direction. The September under is now officially a public trade, and readers of that issue know what the desk thinks of that: the moment the crowd joins the quiet side, the quiet is over.

The two overs are their own tell. One is Saints-Lions, a big number bet bigger. The other is Bears-Panthers over 47 — a total that has already been steamed up three points by the same public that owns 93 percent of the Bears tickets. Opening weekend's most popular combination, in other words, is a single thought held by several million people: Chicago 31, Carolina 13.

sections.title: The Lottery
sections.headline: Props, Scorers and Other Fictions
sections.sub: The parlay economy, itemized
paras: The prop sheet is where the offseason bites people. The most-bet prop in football is David Montgomery's receiving yards — and Montgomery is a Houston Texan now, traded from Detroit this spring, catching passes against the Bills on Sunday. The third is Kenneth Walker's receptions: the Super Bowl MVP who skipped Seattle's ring ceremony debuts for Kansas City on Monday night, and the public wants his hands involved. The fifth is Malik Willis's rushing yards — popular not because he is anyone's backup anymore, but because Miami released its franchise quarterback and paid Willis $67.5 million to run its offense, legs included, starting Sunday in Las Vegas.

And the second-most-bet prop deserves its own paragraph: Cam Ward over half an interception, at plus money. The public is betting a pick out of a quarterback who threw seven all season as a rookie — one of the two cleanest 500-attempt rookie seasons in league history. Maybe the crowd knows something. More likely the crowd likes plus money attached to a plausible sentence, which is the entire economics of the prop menu.

The touchdown lists are pure lottery. Amon-Ra St. Brown at plus money is the respectable anchor; behind him sits Jared Goff at 20-to-1 to score a touchdown — not throw one, score one — which is the kind of ticket printed precisely because it sounds like a story to tell later. The first-scorer list is five names between 7-to-1 and 10-to-1, stapled to a million same-game parlays. None of this is analysis. All of it is inventory — and it all gets graded here anyway.

sections.title: The Verdict
sections.headline: A Census, Not a Strategy
sections.sub: How to read a public board
paras: What is this board actually for? Not for fading — this desk buried that reflex two issues ago, with the receipts: the most-bet college money went 5-0 on opening weekend while the tickets went 3-2, and the public's Week 1 in the NFL last year was a 3-13 disaster. The crowd is neither an ATM nor an oracle. The board is a census: what America believes, itemized with prices attached. This week America believes in the Bears, in one more Rodgers autumn, in quiet games it has now made loud, and in a Lions quarterback finding the end zone with his own legs at 20-to-1.

For the record, the bookmakers' own stated nightmares this week are none of these — the industry's biggest reported futures liability is the Raiders at 125-to-1, and its biggest MVP liability is Saquon Barkley. The public's Sunday card and the books' deep sweats are different documents entirely. This one — every table above — gets graded Monday night, in public, like everything in the file.

The 2026 season opened Wednesday night: 13-10, under 44.5 by three touchdowns. The public's parlay money was on the over. It usually is.

September belongs to the defenses: starters barely play in August, offenses need reps that do not exist yet, and totals are set off last year's scoring. sections.title: The Streak
sections.headline: Twelve and Four, Then One and Oh
sections.sub: The opening week the scoreboard sleeps
paras: Opening week is football's quietest profitable habit. Last September the under went 12-4 across the sixteen games of Week 1 — including an 11-2 rampage through the Sunday slate — and it was not close: Texans-Rams stayed twenty and a half points under the number, Giants-Commanders eighteen and a half. Teams averaged 20.7 points apiece, the lowest-scoring opening week in decades. The year before that was a coin flip; the year before that, another 12-4. The lean is streaky, but it only ever leans one way.

The 2026 edition picked up mid-sentence. Wednesday night's opener closed at 44.5 and produced 23 points — under by three full touchdowns, with a backup quarterback playing fifty-eight minutes and the runner-up throwing the ball to the wrong shirts all fourth quarter. That is 1-0, with fifteen totals still on the board.

sections.title: The Why
sections.headline: Offenses Run on Reps
sections.sub: The mechanics of the September under
paras: The mechanism is not mystical. Starters barely play in the preseason anymore, and offense is the rep-dependent side of football — timing routes, protections, and play sequencing all arrive weeks after tackling does. Defenses have spent two years sitting in two-high shells daring offenses to be patient, and September offenses are not patient; they are rusty. Scoring league-wide has drifted down for half a decade, and it bottoms in the season's first weeks.

The betting version of the story is about lag. Totals open in September priced partly off last season's scoring, and history says the market chases scoring down more slowly than it chases it up — the 2022 season's famous run, when blind unders went 55-38-1 into late October, was exactly that lag being collected. The Week 1 under is the same trade in miniature: the one week a year when the number on the board still remembers last year's offense and the field only has this year's.

sections.title: The Exhibit
sections.headline: Wednesday Night, Entered into Evidence
sections.sub: The opener as thesis statement
paras: If you wanted one game to teach the September under, the opener was it. A champion raising a banner with a backup quarterback by the eleventh minute. A runner-up whose Pro Bowl receiver left in the first half and whose franchise quarterback threw three fourth-quarter interceptions on three straight drives. Seventeen flags. A 7-0 halftime score in a stadium that practices being the loudest place in the sport. Final: 13-10, on a night the recreational money — by DraftKings' own pregame accounting — could not imagine betting anything but the over.

The desk's referee issue took the under at 44.5 and graded it won by morning; the sharp public commentary leaned the same way. The parlay economy leaned over, as it structurally must — nobody builds a same-game parlay out of punts — and paid for the seats.

sections.title: The Verdict
sections.headline: Thin, Real, and Rented
sections.sub: What the September under is actually worth
paras: Now the desk does what the desk does to its own thesis. The long-run Week 1 under rate is about 54.9 percent since 2015 — real, and about two points of margin over break-even, which is an edge the way a sweater is a coat. The books shade September totals low on purpose; the year after the last 12-4, the week graded a coin flip, which is exactly what chasing a famous number gets you. And this year the crowd is arriving: when 87 percent of the money at a major book is on an under, the trade is no longer contrarian — it is merely early to its own funeral.

So the read is the one this desk keeps arriving at: the lean is a reason to like low totals you already like — backup quarterbacks, wind, teams whose offenses are installing rather than executing — and no reason at all to bet sixteen unders like it is 2022. Twelve and four was last year. One and oh is one game. The other fifteen get graded here, in public, by Monday night.

sections.title: The Assignment
sections.headline: The Man in the Middle
sections.sub: Who holds the whistle tonight, and what his games do

stats.l: To the under in 2025 — best in the league

paras: Tonight's kickoff game has three teams on the field: the champions, the runners-up, and Adrian Hill's crew — confirmed by Football Zebras for the opener, with four officials working their 24th NFL season behind him. And Hill is the kind of referee the betting internet notices. His games lean under: 62 wins, 50 losses and a push for under bettors across his career as a white hat, and a league-best 7–2 to the under last season.

Now, the number making the rounds — 12–5 to the under in primetime, 71 percent. The desk went looking for its source and found none: no stats site, no book, no outlet publishes it. That does not make it false; primetime splits live in databases the public reads secondhand. It makes it ungradeable — and this desk grades. So here is what is actually citable: the career lean above, the 2025 league lead, and the backdrop that primetime games league-wide have gone under at roughly 56 percent over recent seasons. The direction of the claim survives. The decimal does not.

The market, for the record, is not acting on any of it: the total opened at 44.5 and has not moved an inch all summer, with reported action on it close to even — and the recreational money expected on the over, riding two top-three scoring offenses. If the under is the sharp side tonight, it is a quiet one.

sections.title: The Rocket Scientist
sections.headline: From Goddard to the Goal Line
sections.sub: The most overqualified man in stripes
paras: Hill's path to the white hat is the best bio in officiating. Electrical engineering and computer science at the University at Buffalo. NASA contract work at Goddard Space Flight Center in the nineties. Principal software engineer at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, designing fault-management systems for spacecraft — the code that decides what a satellite does when everything goes wrong. Baltimore's Engineer of the Year, 2006. Then he answered a newspaper ad and started calling youth football for thirteen dollars a game.

He joined the NFL as a line judge in 2010, took over a crew in 2019, and has spent seventeen seasons applying fault-management logic to Sunday chaos — including to himself: carted off on a Thursday night last November with a non-contact leg injury, back for the playoffs anyway. Tonight he opens the season in the loudest building in the sport.

sections.title: The Grudge
sections.headline: Same Crew, Same Coach
sections.sub: October 12, 2025 — the receipts
paras: One more reason New England knows this crew: last October, in Hill's only Patriots assignment of the season, an offensive pass interference call on Stefon Diggs wiped out a 61-yard Drake Maye touchdown — part of roughly 113 yards and a score erased on the day. The Patriots won anyway, and Mike Vrabel still called the officiating 'comical.' Hill answered questions through a pool report. Tonight is the first meeting since.

The crew's profile explains the friction. In 2025 it threw the second-most flags per game in football — 17.9 — but with a particular flavor: offensive holding at a third above the league rate, while unnecessary roughness and offsides ran far below it. Technique flags, not mayhem flags. That is the desk's read on the under lean, too — a crew that flags holding kills drives, and dead drives kill totals. Treat that as analysis, not gospel: the causal story is tidy, and tidy stories are how referee stats get oversold.

sections.title: The Genre
sections.headline: Betting the Stripes
sections.sub: A short history of referee angles
paras: Referee handicapping is a standing genre now — weekly 'zebra reports,' per-crew databases, assignment trackers that race the books every Wednesday when Football Zebras posts the crews. The canon records all trace to the same trends databases: Tony Corrente, the most profitable under referee ever published at 102–80–4; Carl Cheffers and his home-team splits; Shawn Smith, under whom home teams covered 17 of 49 — and who refereed the Super Bowl these two teams just played.

The skeptic case is arithmetic. A referee works seventeen games a year; even Corrente's famous 56 percent, across a decade of games, sits within shouting distance of a coin flip. League-wide studies — ESPN's penalty database work, the Harvard Sports Analysis Collective's scrape of twenty thousand flags — find crew-to-crew differences in penalties are real, but no systematic bias a bettor can eat with. And the books read the same pages: one study of the legal era found totals already drift with a crew's penalty rate. The edge, where it exists, is a point of shade, priced by Thursday.

Why does the genre survive its own math? Because of the one time it was real. Tim Donaghy — an NBA referee betting his own games — produced a stretch of ten straight officiated games where the line moved a point and a half before tip and the big money cashed all ten. He went to prison, the NBA published the Pedowitz Report, and referee data became a permanent fixture of betting culture: the whistle is the one variable on the floor that once provably moved the number.

sections.title: The Verdict
sections.headline: A Feather, Not an Anchor
sections.sub: What a referee lean is actually worth
paras: The under case tonight: a referee with the league's best under record last season, a technique-flag crew, a banner-night ceremony, two teams that have not played a snap that counts since February, and a league-wide primetime under lean. The over case: the two best scoring offenses on the field in this game a year ago, both upgraded, the simulation models leaning over, and the recreational money coming in behind them.

The desk's rule for referee angles is the same as for every trend in this series: they are for reading, not for anchoring. A crew lean is worth a half-point of respect — a reason to like a number you already like, never a reason to bet one you don't. Tonight the desk's two issues point the same direction anyway: the runner-up and the points, and the quiet side of a total that has not moved since May. Both get graded by midnight, in public, like everything in the file.

Postscript, Thursday morning: Seattle 13, New England 10. Under 44.5 by twenty-one and a half points — Sam Darnold left on the opening drive, Drake Maye threw three fourth-quarter interceptions, and the crew threw seventeen flags, four-tenths off its yearly average. The feather landed. The file notes, in fairness, that a backup quarterback had more to do with it than the whistle — and that grading honestly is the entire point of this desk.

Tonight the trend kicks off the season itself: the Patriots, fresh off losing Super Bowl LX by sixteen, open at the Seahawks — only the third Week 1 Super Bowl rematch ever — as three-point underdogs on banner night.

sections.title: The Trend
sections.headline: Nobody Covers the Morning After
sections.sub: Twenty-six Septembers of runners-up
paras: The team that loses the Super Bowl spends seven months hearing how close it came — and then, in its first game back, fails to cover the spread. It is one of the most published trends in football betting: by the most common accounting, Super Bowl losers are six covers against twenty misses in Week 1 since 2000. Different books grade the pushes differently — published versions run from 4–19 to 7–19 — but every version agrees on the shape.

And the shape is the real story. From 2000 through 2011 the runner-up went 0–12 against the number — not a single cover in twelve years, a run that ended entire theories about market efficiency. Since 2012 the record is roughly a coin flip, because bookmakers read the same trend pages bettors do and started pricing the hangover in. The zombie version of the stat still walks — but the number it built now lives inside the line.

The straight-up record is hardly better: the runner-up has lost its opener outright more often than not since 2000, and the two most recent losers — the 2024 49ers and 2025 Chiefs — each followed the opener to a 6–11 season and a missed postseason.

sections.title: The Wreckage
sections.headline: How They Lose
sections.sub: The canon of the hangover
paras: The genre has classics. In 2008 the Patriots, a 16.5-point favorite over Kansas City seven months after their perfect season died, lost Tom Brady's knee fifteen minutes into the opener and won by seven — the most catastrophic no-cover in the file. In 2011 the Steelers walked into Baltimore and lost 35–7. In 2015 the Seahawks lost in overtime to a Rams team bound for 7–9, complete with a failed short-yardage run that made every viewer think of the goal line in Glendale.

The sharpest precedent for tonight is 2016: the NFL opened the season with the Super Bowl 50 rematch, Carolina at Denver. The Panthers led by ten in the fourth quarter, gave it all back, and lost 21–20 when Graham Gano missed from fifty with four seconds left — the champion won the game and the runner-up, laying three, covered nothing. And last season the trend collected again in São Paulo: the Chiefs, three-point favorites over the Chargers, lost the opener — the first tremor of a 6–11 collapse.

sections.title: The Why
sections.headline: The Shortest Summer
sections.sub: What actually causes it
paras: The explanations are mundane, which is why they persist. The Super Bowl loser gets the shortest offseason in the sport with none of the consolation. Its coordinators get hired away, its veterans get poached, and its market price stays inflated by the fact that everyone watched it play in February — the public overrates the runner-up, so the number does too. The quantified version: Super Bowl losers underperform their preseason win totals by about a full win on average, and when the quarterback misses time, by nearly four.

The honest counterweight: the season-long 'curse' is softer than the Week 1 stat. About two-thirds of Super Bowl losers still make the playoffs the next year, and one — the 2018 Patriots — turned the hangover into a title. But the modern run is grim: the last seven runners-up beat their win total once, and the last two finished 6–11. Week 1 is where the season after starts telling you which kind it will be.

sections.title: The Test
sections.headline: Tonight, in Seattle
sections.sub: The trend kicks off the season
paras: Tonight the trend is not a footnote to the schedule — it is the schedule. The Patriots, who lost Super Bowl LX to Seattle 29–13, open the season at Lumen Field on banner night, in only the third Week 1 Super Bowl rematch in league history (the 1970 Vikings avenged theirs; the 2016 Panthers did not). The line opened Seattle −4.5 in May and has been bet down to −3 — barely a point off the Super Bowl closing number, as if the market never left Santa Clara.

The case for the runner-up is real: a 14–3 team that added A.J. Brown to an MVP runner-up quarterback, coached by the reigning Coach of the Year — against a champion raising its banner without its Super Bowl MVP, Kenneth Walker III having taken Kansas City's money and skipped the ring ceremony. The case against is this entire file, plus a schedule that turns first-place hard after an easy 2025.

Here is what makes tonight the perfect laboratory: the mirror trend points the same way. Defending champions are 17–4 straight-up in kickoff games — and cover almost none of them, roughly one in five in recent years. The books, reportedly heavy with Patriots moneyline action, need the middle: Seattle by one or two. That is precisely how the 2016 rematch settled. If it happens again, the champion wins, the runner-up covers, and both trends limp on — which is the most on-brand possible result for a stat the market already ate.

The desk's read is the same one this section always lands on: the number tonight already contains the hangover — what it may not contain is a banner-night champion that never covers these games, and a runner-up built more like an heir than a hangover.

One postscript from our own case files: the last time the Patriots played a game this big, Drake had a million dollars on them, lost it, and announced he was off sports betting. He is 4–8 lifetime on Super Bowl wagers, and as of press time has not been sighted on this one. Make of that omen what you will — it gets graded by midnight, like everything else in the file.

Postscript, Thursday morning: Seattle 13, New England 10 — by exactly three. The runner-up did not cover and did not lose; the champion won its banner game and covered nothing; the books' middle never came and the spread pushed at the closing number. Two tired trends walked into Seattle, and both walked out alive without cashing a ticket — the champ's kickoff no-cover run extends, the loser's hangover file adds a push, and the record is now 6-20-1. The desk notes it was the second pick in this publication's first week to lose by exactly its number. The margins are developing a sense of humor.

sections.title: The Consensus
sections.headline: Ninety Percent of Everything
sections.sub: The splits, as the week opened
paras: Sunday afternoon in Charlotte, the Chicago Bears open their season as three-point road favorites, and America has already voted. At BetMGM — by the book's own accounting — Bears spread bets were running at 93 percent, the most lopsided game of the entire Week 1 board. Splits reports put the money at 91 percent there, with DraftKings at 83 percent of tickets and 94 percent of dollars, and BetRivers at 75 and 91. However you count it, this is the most public side of opening week.

It is not alone — the whole board leans one way. The Cowboys are drawing 95 percent of spread money against the Giants; the Rams are a 79 percent side in the league's first game in Australia; the Jaguars have been called the clearest public team on the board. But nothing matches the Bears, whose over has moved three full points on its own — 44.5 to 47.5 — as bettors, in the words of DraftKings' Johnny Avello, chase an offense that scored twenty-five a game with a plus-22 turnover ratio a year ago.

sections.title: The Case
sections.headline: Why They Believe
sections.sub: The best story in football, one year in
paras: The confidence is not irrational. Ben Johnson's first season in Chicago produced an 11–6 record, the NFC North, and the franchise's first playoff win since 2010 — a wild-card comeback from 21–3 down against Green Bay. Caleb Williams set the franchise single-season passing record and led the league with seven fourth-quarter comebacks. The market has followed: Chicago opened this season with its shortest Super Bowl price since 2019.

And there is poetry in the matchup. A meaningful share of this Bears roster exists because of Carolina — the 2023 trade in which the Panthers surrendered the picks and players that became Chicago's core, to draft Bryce Young. Young, whose career year in 2025 won a soft NFC South at 8–9, is the quarterback standing across from the franchise his old team accidentally built.

The bear case, so to speak, exists too: Bill Barnwell made Chicago his top regression candidate for 2026, and the team the public remembers from November is not the one that showed up in last year's opener — more on that presently.

sections.title: The Openers
sections.headline: The Bears in September
sections.sub: A decade of first Sundays
paras: Here is the franchise the public is laying three with: 3–7 straight-up in its last ten season openers. Six consecutive opener losses from 2014 through 2019. No back-to-back opener wins since 2012 and 2013. Last September, in Ben Johnson's debut, the Bears led Minnesota by eleven in the fourth quarter of the opener and lost on twenty-one unanswered points, with twelve penalties for 127 yards. The opener they won the year before, the offense scored no touchdowns at all — a blocked punt and a pick-six did it.

The sharper cut: in the last decade the Bears have been favored in an opener three times, and lost two of them outright — at home. In 2019, as champions of the division and favored by exactly three — the number the public is laying now — they scored three points, total, against Green Bay. And in all that time they have never once been what they are on Sunday: a road favorite in Week 1. By the findable lines, it has not happened in at least sixteen years.

sections.title: The Other Side
sections.headline: The Worst Week 1 Team in Football
sections.sub: Which is not the same as a bad bet
paras: The team catching the points is, by the record, the worst opening-day franchise in the league: eleven wins against twenty losses in Week 1, and none at all since 2021. That is the stat the 93 percent are betting on. The stats they are betting against: Carolina went 6–2 against the spread as a home underdog last season, won the NFC South, and exercised the fifth-year option on a quarterback coming off a career year.

The situational math leans the same way. Week 1 underdogs have covered at 53 percent since 2000, and since 2019 the sharpest slice of that edge is exactly this spot — home dogs of three points or fewer, covering at 57.6 percent. Offseason narratives are at their loudest in Week 1 and their least tested; last September the public went 3–13 against the spread in the opening week before recovering to roughly break even on the year. The prediction markets are quietly less sure than the sportsbook lobbies: Kalshi has priced Carolina's chances near 41 percent, better than the moneyline implies.

sections.title: The Number
sections.headline: Held at Three
sections.sub: What the price is telling you
paras: Roughly fifteen percent of NFL games land on exactly three — the most common final margin in football, nearly double the next number. It is the one line bookmakers hate to cross: move to three and a half with this much one-way money and a Bears field-goal win sides or middles the book on the most-landed number in the sport. So the books have mostly held — the market has straddled two and a half and three all week, taxing the juice instead of moving — which means somebody is willingly carrying a nine-figure-percentage position against the most popular bet in America rather than pay to get off the number.

What does the fade math say? The canonical backtests — fading sides with 80-plus percent of tickets — showed 54 to 57 percent, on data that mostly predates 2016; the edge has compressed since. And this game has the wrinkle the studies never resolved: tickets and money agree here, which the folk wisdom calls a weaker fade than a divergence. The two most famous 90/90 games in recent memory split the argument — Kansas City covered one in a walk in 2018, then lost one outright as a bigger consensus in 2021.

So the desk will not pretend the arithmetic settles it. The public has the best team. The fade has the number, the venue, the situational record, and a decade of Bears Septembers. That is what makes it the bet of the week — and either way, it gets graded Sunday night, in public, like everything else in the file.

The most-popular sides by ticket count went three-and-two, sunk by Indiana laying forty and a half and an Oregon team that let Boise State hang around. The most-bet sides by dollars went five for five, and the fifth entry was not chalk at all: North Texas, catching that same forty and a half in Bloomington, covered by four and a half points.

The lists are not folklore. At BetMGM, LSU was the most-bet team of the entire Saturday slate by both tickets and money, and cashed by forty-one. At DraftKings, Alabama drew ninety percent of the tickets and ninety-two percent of the handle and covered by ten and a half. sections.title: The Weekend
sections.headline: Chalk, Delivered
sections.sub: How the books actually lost it
paras: The slate was built for it: twenty of the twenty-four games involving Top 25 programs closed with spreads of twenty points or more, eleven of them thirty or more. The big brands delivered in big ways — LSU by forty-one in Lane Kiffin's debut, Texas by fifty-two, Alabama by thirty-eight — and, in the words of FOX's weekend recap, customers found success with "pretty much every other big favorite easily covering."

Then there was Michigan. A twenty-seven-and-a-half-point favorite over Western Michigan, trailing 12–6 in the final second, granted a do-over when officials put one second back on the clock — and Bryce Underwood threw a Hail Mary touchdown to win 13–12. Nobody near the spread cared; the moneyline parlays did. BetMGM had taken six times more moneyline bets on Michigan than its opponent, most of them parlay legs, and the replayed snap flipped the book's result on the game. One bettor at Fanatics had put ten thousand dollars on Michigan live at 28-to-1 when the loss looked sealed; the do-over paid $290,000. At Hard Rock, a $1.06 twenty-leg parlay cashed for $130,000.

For balance, the books took Thursday: Washington, Georgia Tech and Auburn — the most public sides of the opening slate — all failed to cover, Georgia Tech losing outright on a last-minute touchdown and a blocked field goal. Readers of this desk will recognize that side. It headlined a certain 2–8 card.

sections.title: The Myth
sections.headline: Nobody Is Balancing the Book
sections.sub: Where fade-the-public came from, and why it died
paras: The fade rests on a folk model: books balance action, shade lines toward the crowd, and profit on the vig — so the other side holds value. The first half is simply false, and bookmakers say so themselves. Asked in 2022 whether books balance bets to lock in profit, the Westgate's Jay Kornegay called the idea "an urban legend." Red Rock's Chuck Esposito: "somewhat of a myth." The South Point's Chris Andrews: "rarely the reality."

The respectable core of the fade was real once. The economist Steven Levitt showed in 2004 that books deliberately carry lopsided positions and price against bettor biases, boosting profits an estimated twenty to thirty percent over a balanced book — and in that era, extreme contrarian positions backtested profitably. But the edge assumed slow, soft lines. Modern prices are set by market-makers and moved by sharp money, not ticket counts; the crowd's tickets barely bend the number. What is left to fade is mostly nothing: over the long run the public wins roughly forty-eight percent of its spread bets — a coin flip minus the price, not an ATM.

sections.title: The Precedent
sections.headline: The Public Has Done This Before
sections.sub: When the crowd breaks the industry
paras: A public weekend is not even unusual anymore. In October 2021, NFL favorites ran the table on an early slate and Caesars' head of trading described it in two words: "a bloodbath." The 2024 NFL season went further — FanDuel's parent called it "the most customer friendly since the launch of online sports betting, with the highest rate of favourites winning in nearly 20 years," and warned of a $370 million revenue hit. DraftKings cut guidance by a quarter-billion. Nevada's books lost money on football in December 2024 — the first losing football month in twelve years.

And here is the other half of the ledger, the reason the books keep the lights on: even in that disaster year, the American industry held 9.3 percent of everything wagered, on record revenue of $13.7 billion. The public wins weekends. The hold wins years. Both of those facts were on display this weekend, and neither one is a betting strategy.

sections.title: The Signal
sections.headline: Watch the Money, Not the Crowd
sections.sub: What Week 1 actually taught
paras: The week's real tell was the divergence. Indiana drew one-way ticket action at forty and a half — "They're laying the 40 points," Caesars' football trader said — yet the price got bought back toward thirty-nine and a half. The line moved against the tickets, and the tickets lost. In Buffalo's opener, sixty-nine percent of tickets took the Bulldogs while eighty-two percent of the money took Albany; the spread collapsed from twenty-four and a half to eighteen and a half. When tickets and dollars disagree, the dollars are usually somebody who knows something.

Even that is not a system. The only published backtest of fading heavy money in college football found an edge — fifty-five percent — but only in the games where the line moved with the money; where the price stood still, the signal vanished. The splits themselves come from a single recreational book's customers, a keyhole view of a market whose sharpest money never appears in them. The lesson of Week 1 is not that the public is sharp now, or that the fade is back. It is older and simpler: crowds are noise, prices are information, and people are records. The desk grades the people.

call.title: The fade is dead.
call.note: Long live the fade — of the right people. The public is not an ATM, and never was. Records are. That is what the case files are for.

paras: Every Saturday morning, Steve Coughlin — Stanford Steve to anyone with a television — sits at the College GameDay desk and gives out numbers. Unlike most people who do that for a living, his have been written down. All of them, for twelve years.

Cole's Gameday Blog has tracked every public pick Coughlin has made since 2014 — GameDay, ESPN's betting shows, SportsCenter, all of it. The ledger reads 648 wins, 529 losses and 24 pushes against the spread: 55.1 percent over 1,201 picks, which at standard pricing works out to more than 60 units of profit. The break-even line for a bettor paying −110 is 52.4 percent. Holding three points above it for over a decade is not variance. It is a career.

Among every analyst the site has tracked to a thousand or more picks, no one matches his win rate. Only one picker on the entire board has banked more total units, and it took him three times the volume to do it. The peaks are real, too: a 57–29 season in 2018 worth nearly 23 units, a 53–30 debut in 2014, and a 63–50 start to the current season that already sits 7.4 units in the black.

sections.title: The Bonus
sections.headline: A Ladder Worth Three Million
sections.sub: What LSU owes Lane Kiffin for winning
paras: Lane Kiffin's LSU contract pays him bonuses that climb with every step of a playoff run — $750,000 for getting the Tigers into the College Football Playoff, scaling to $3 million if he wins the national championship. Somebody is on the hook for that money the moment the confetti falls.

Historically, that somebody buys insurance. Schools lay off the risk of their coach's success the way airlines lay off fuel prices — through specialist underwriters, most famously at Lloyd's of London. What changed this month is where the hedge showed up: in public, on an exchange, at prices anyone can look up.

The cost of the position was $662,050. The maximum payout, if the Tigers run the table, is $3 million. That is not a round number by accident; it is, to the dollar, Kiffin's championship bonus.

The trades trace to Game Point Capital, a sports insurance firm whose business is protecting schools from the happy disaster of a coach hitting his incentives. Kalshi's chief executive announced a partnership with the firm in February. Similar third-party positions appeared on South Carolina's season a month earlier.

The arithmetic on the first rung shows the machinery plainly: if LSU makes the playoff, the position pays $837,500 — more than covering the $750,000 check the school owes its coach for getting there. Every deeper run pays more, exactly as the obligation grows.

The cruelty is in the margins. Georgia Tech, laying six and a half against Colorado, lost outright — a touchdown pass with forty-two seconds left, then a blocked field goal on the final play. Furman, catching forty-six and a half at Tennessee, lost 56–9: a cover dead by half a point. And the finale landed on the number itself — Florida State, catching three, beaten by exactly three. Eleven picks, and not one clean exit.

sections.title: The Body of Work
sections.headline: It Was Not the First
sections.sub: Fifteen seasons of receipts
paras: The record has a literature. In 2017, the Ohio State site Eleven Warriors spent a full season betting ten dollars against every pick he published and finished 83–67 on the fade — a fourteen percent profit, chronicled week by week and toasted by Deadspin. In 2024 and again in 2025, the Minnesota blog The Daily Gopher ran the same experiment, finished 96–80 and then 94–87 betting the opposite, and donated the winnings to charity. Three season-long fades, three profits.

His own columns tell the same story in the first person. The 2024 season, by his own running count, went from 'a disastrous first two months' at 54–71, to 74–90 at Thanksgiving, to 92–111 by the night of the title game. Last season he stood 82–82 in late November before a three-and-nine week erased the year's work. And in 2019, on Fox's own daily gambling show, he opened with thirteen consecutive losing picks.

He knows. 'My college football picks have been such a disaster this year, you may be better off fading all my picks this week,' he posted in November 2024 — and three weeks later captioned a card, 'So feel free to take the opposite.' At OutKick, his betting show with the Vegas handicapper Kelly Stewart was titled, with no apparent irony, The Fade.

Against all of this stands his own assessment: a claim, made on air, of winning sixty percent of his college bets across a three-year stretch. The handicapper-watchdog site CapperReviews noted that no documented professional has held sixty percent over any three-year period, and publicly challenged him to produce the ledger. The ledger has not appeared.

sections.title: The House
sections.headline: The House Publishes His Picks
sections.sub: The business of being wrong
paras: None of this has been bad for business. Travis left OutKick in June and launched a new media company, Sport & State, in August — with Hard Rock Bet as an equity investor and its exclusive sportsbook partner. His Week 1 card ran on the sportsbook's own site, under the headline '11 Winners Starting Thursday Night.'

Sit with the mechanics of that: a sportsbook part-owns the company whose founder publishes picks, and hosts the picks itself. Whatever the record does, the action arrives. There has never been a cleaner illustration of the first rule of betting media — the picks are not the product. The handle is.
Which is the argument for keeping the receipts somewhere the house doesn't own.

sections.title: The Curse
sections.headline: First, the Folklore
sections.sub: A decade of losses he never bet on
paras: Before there was a ledger, there was a superstition. It grew up around Kentucky basketball in 2013, when Drake attached himself to a Calipari program that kept reaching Final Fours and never winning one. It went mainstream at the 2015 US Open, when he sat courtside as Serena Williams — two wins from the calendar Grand Slam — lost to Roberta Vinci in the semifinal. Serena, asked about it the next year, refused the premise: 'I'm the one who's playing, who's making mistakes or making winners. I'm not one to blame anyone else for anything.'

The internet was less rigorous. By 2019 the curse was a beat of its own: a PSG defender posted a photo with him and lost 5–1 the next day; AS Roma's official account jokingly banned its players from pictures with him until season's end; Anthony Joshua tweeted a photo captioned 'Bout to break the curse' and promptly suffered the biggest upset in modern heavyweight history. The night he walked Conor McGregor to the cage at UFC 229 — no bet, just an Irish flag — Khabib mauled him. The Raptors' 2019 title, with Drake courtside in a Dell Curry jersey, was supposed to be the exorcism.
Then, in February 2022, the folklore got a bankroll. He signed with the crypto sportsbook Stake and started posting the slips.

sections.title: The Ledger
sections.headline: Forty Million Dollars, Graded
sections.sub: Every posted slip since February 2022
paras: The independent tracker thedrakecurse.com has collected every publicly posted or reported bet since his first — $1.26 million in Bitcoin on Super Bowl LVI, February 13, 2022 — converting the crypto to dollars at the day of the wager. The file, as of its July update: 88 bets, $40.2 million staked, $37.2 million returned. Thirty-two wins, fifty-six losses. A 36.4 percent strike rate at an average stake of four hundred fifty-seven thousand dollars.

The arc is the story. He survived a seven-bet, $3.8 million losing streak in the fall of 2022 and still closed the year up $307,000. Then came 2023 — Jon Jones by submission at +580, Adesanya by knockout at +360, a million on Gervonta Davis — and by July he sat at plus $4.58 million, the high-water mark. He has been giving it back ever since: down $1.59 million in 2024, down $1.78 million in 2025, and down $3.27 million through July of this year, when the file hit its all-time low.

Here is the part the memes get wrong: the curse is mostly a myth. Of his fifty-six losses, the tracker counts only eleven 'actual curses' — favorites he backed that fell. Israel Adesanya accounts for three of them by himself. The rest of the file is something more ordinary and more expensive: long-odds moneylines at enormous stakes. The favorites don't die because he bets them. The dogs just don't come in.

paras: The wins are real, and they are spectacular: a three-hundred-nine-thousand-dollar, three-leg Game 7 parlay in May 2022 that returned $2.67 million; Jon Jones by submission at nearly six to one; $1.15 million on the Chiefs in Super Bowl LVIII, posted with the caption "I can't bet against the Swifties," which cashed for $1.2 million.

The losses are the genre's masterpieces. He bet $1 million on Argentina to win the 2022 World Cup final in ninety minutes; Argentina won the World Cup, on penalties, and the ticket died at 3–3. Four years later he bet $1.5 million on Argentina to win the 2026 final inside ninety — it was 0–0 at the whistle, and Spain won in extra time. The same bet, the same beat, two World Cups apart. In between: $1.6 million on Adesanya the night Pereira took his belt, a million on the Maple Leafs in a Game 7 they lost by five, and a million on Conor McGregor's comeback, which lasted sixty-nine seconds.
This summer, for balance, he also bet one dollar on Morocco. It won him forty-one cents.

sections.title: Not Like Us
sections.headline: The Kendrick Chapter
sections.sub: April 30, 2024, and everything after
paras: On April 30, 2024, Kendrick Lamar released 'Euphoria,' and the most famous feud in rap history began grading Drake's slips in real time. On 'Meet the Grahams' the accusation was explicit: 'You got gamblin' problems, drinkin' problems, pill-poppin' and spendin' problems.' Drake's response was sarcasm — but the tracker's response was arithmetic: since the day 'Euphoria' dropped, it counts $7.2 million in betting losses.

The era produced the file's cruelest footnote. In July 2024 he put $300,000 on Canada to upset Argentina in the Copa América semifinal. Argentina won 2–0, and the Argentine national team's official account posted four words: 'Not like us, not with us.'

By June 2025 he was publishing the damage himself — an Instagram story showing $124.5 million wagered and $8.2 million lost in a single month, captioned 'Gotta share the other side of gambling.' Whatever the beef settled, the ledger's verdict arrived on its own schedule.

sections.title: The House
sections.headline: The Slips Are the Ad
sections.sub: What the bets are for
paras: Every one of those posted slips is a screenshot from Stake, the crypto casino that signed him in 2022 in a deal the Financial Times has reported at roughly $100 million a year — a figure neither side has ever confirmed. The bets are content; the content is marketing. When he swore off sports betting after February's million-dollar Patriots loss — 'sticking to what I know' — he was back with three more seven-figure wagers by July.

The relationship is stormier than the feed suggests. In August 2025 he announced a gambling break, accused Stake of blocking his withdrawals and called its co-founder a snake on a livestream; by October he was betting there again. And in October 2025 a Missouri class action named Drake, Adin Ross and Stake, alleging among other things that the company fronts its stars house money — that the famous losses are, in effect, advertising. Stake disputes the suits, and called a Bloomberg analysis of its streamers' unusual slot luck 'categorically incorrect.' The courts will grade those claims; this desk only grades the slips.
Either way, the conclusion is the same one printed on the cover: whether the money is his or the house's, the record is public, and the record is 32–56.

call.note: Down $3.06 million all-time, $7.2 million since 'Euphoria.' By his own testimony: 'My slips do not cash out. But one day I'm gonna have a parlay that's insane.' Until that day, the file stays open.

sections.title: The Hedge
sections.headline: Two Sides of One Trade
sections.sub: Why the losses do not matter
paras: Jim McIngvale bets like nobody else on earth: nine-figure furniture promotions hedged with the largest sportsbook wagers ever written. The tracked record reads three wins and seventeen losses across roughly eighty-six million dollars in reported stakes — and he is up twenty-three and a half million. That is not a typo. It is a hedge.

Every giant ticket backs a 'win your mattress free' promotion at his Gallery Furniture stores. If the team loses, the promotion money stays home and the ticket is the cost of the marketing. If the team wins, the sportsbooks fund the refunds. The sportsbook money and the store money are two sides of one trade — which is why a 3–17 record can be a triumph.

Knowing the difference between a bad record and a bad bet is the whole game. This file is the proof.
